title: 2025-2027 New York City Construction Outlook Report
plain_title: Three-year forecast for New York City construction
what_they_audited: A forecast report from the New York Building Congress projecting construction spending, employment and building activity in New York City through 2027, closing with a set of policy proposals aimed at federal, state and city government.
background: The report tracks residential, non-residential and government construction spending in the five boroughs, drawing on federal spending data and city building permit records.

findings.plain: Construction spending is projected to hold roughly flat once inflation is taken into account.
findings.quote: In today’s dollars, spending is expected to dip from roughly $74 billion in 2025 to about $69 billion in 2026 before edging back up to $75.3 billion in 2027

findings.plain: Construction employment is projected to stay near current levels through 2027.
findings.quote: The Building Congress anticipates employment in the construction of buildings, heavy and civil engineering, and specialty trades to total 139,000 jobs in 2025, and 140,000 in 2026 and

findings.plain: Residential permits are expected to fall sharply from 2024 while remaining well above 2023.
findings.quote: In the residential sector, building permits are expected to be issued for nearly 19,000 new units in 2025, onethird less than in 2024, but still double the volume of 2023.

findings.plain: Borrowing costs are named as a main reason activity has slowed.
findings.quote: Higher borrowing costs remain a key reason for reduced industry activity.

findings.plain: The report says firms are holding back on large spending until conditions become clearer.
findings.quote: Many firms and private sector investors are choosing to delay large expenditures until conditions become more predictable or until interest rates are cut.

recommendations: Release Surface Transportation Reauthorization funding quickly and ensure New York gets a share matching its population, the size of its public transit systems and what it contributes to the federal tax base and gross domestic product.
Establish a federal infrastructure bank so that infrastructure investment continues nationwide.
Improve and reform project delivery methods and procurement so projects move faster and with more flexibility.
Streamline project approvals through land use reform, including the housing measures in the City of Yes plan.
Reform permitting and National Environmental Policy Act review to speed up environmental reviews, through legislation such as the RESTART Act.
Invest further in workforce training and development at all levels of government.
Maintain robust capital budgets and adequate staffing at state and city agencies, including public authorities.
Advance and broaden opportunities for minority- and women-owned business enterprises and develop policies that give those firms meaningful economic prospects.
Broaden and expand the development incentives in the Affordable Neighborhoods for New Yorkers tax incentive program, known as 485-x.
Invest in citywide resiliency measures to protect at-risk communities and critical infrastructure from extreme weather.
Invest significantly in energy infrastructure and grid networks, including battery energy storage systems, to keep energy reliable as usage grows.
